## In this session

- What is a **model** in the context of DH research
- **Conceptual modelling**: producing a conceptualisation of a domain of interest
- Choosing data structures: **HTML/XML**, **key-value**, **relational** and **graph** data structures
- Two exercises

## Conceptual modelling

What is the point of view of [@flanders2018]: what do the authors state, what do they omit?

The essence of the ontoing digital transformation is converting available information into digital data using a model.
This has a huge potential in view of developing new knowledge production methods in HSS. 

But what is a model?
In science, a model is defined as a simplified yet equivalent representation of an original phenomenon, highlighting specific characteristics for a particular purpose. Models are used to explain, analyse or predict complex phenomena. 
Cf. the entry [*Model* in Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model) and compare the versions in different languages.

In humanities, creating a [conceptual model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conceptual_model) of a domain of interest is an essential step that provides a clear understanding of the research endeavour and should take place before any choice of methodology and technology used in data producion. 

Cf. [these slides](https://github.com/Sciences-historiques-numeriques/information-systems/blob/main/slides/Beretta-Conceptual-Modelling-and-Research-Cycle-1-0.pdf) that will be commented during the course.



### Data structures kinds: 

You can implement the conceptual model of a domain of interest using any of these data structures and technologies; each has its own specific advantages and limitations. 
We will explore the possibilities offered by relational databases, with a particular focus on the SQLite technology.

- HTML / XML / TEI: markup, semantic trees [this will be presented and discussed in sessions 6 and 7]
- [JSON](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JSON): key-value structure, lists, collections
  - [NoSQL databases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NoSQL), e.g. [Apache Cassandra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apache_Cassandra)
- [SQL Databases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SQL): tables, columns and relations
  - [PostgreSQL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PostgreSQL), [SQLite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SQLite)
- [Graph Databases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_database): nodes, properties and arcs
  - Labeled-property graphs: [neo4j](https://neo4j.com/graphgists/test-test/); PostgreSQL with the [Apache AGE extension](https://age.apache.org/overview) and in future  versions implementing directly the [GQL standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_Query_Language)
  - RDF [this will be presented and discussed in session 5]

## Reflection: diversity of domains in the humanities

Different disciplines model different things, you can build conceptual models for any of them, before you choose a methodology or technology:

- **Texts** — corpora, text structure, language, topics, information extraction
- **Prosopography** — people, roles, relations, uncertain identity across sources
- **Materiality** — objects, substances, condition, provenance, physical description



## Exercise 2: Conceptualising some aspects of prosopography

Begin with a research question or type of analysis that you would undertake:

- map the birthplaces of your population and their development over time.
- analyse teacher-student relationships using social network analysis.
- analyse networks of organisations through memberships at different times.

How would you model the information needed to create these analyses?

List the information required and sketch a conceptual model on paper.

The Lab introduces [draw.io](https://app.diagrams.net/) (as VSCode extension: Draw.io Integration by Henning Dieterichs), [QuickDBD](https://app.quickdatabasediagrams.com/) and DBeaver the same week.
